name: How much contingency should I budget for an attached ADU?

mainEntity.name: What extra budget should I set aside for hidden structural, utility, or permit surprises during an attached ADU project?
mainEntity.text: What extra budget should I set aside for hidden structural, utility, or permit surprises during an attached ADU project?

acceptedAnswer.text: Attached ADUs frequently uncover hidden conditions once demolition begins, so contingency planning matters more than most owners expect. Common surprises include outdated electrical systems, weak framing, foundation issues, plumbing conflicts, drainage problems, and finish repairs where the new addition connects to the old house. A typical contingency range is often around 10% to 20% of construction cost, but older homes, slope sites, or heavily remodeled properties may need more. The reason is simple: an attached project depends on an existing structure that may not match the drawings perfectly. Homeowners should ask contractors and designers what risks are most likely on their specific site, rather than using a generic percentage only. A strong proposal should identify likely allowances for structural upgrades, utility changes, and finish tie-ins. Contingency is not just emergency money; it is part of a realistic project budget. It can be the difference between finishing the ADU smoothly and stalling midway through construction.
acceptedAnswer.description: A contingency budget is important because attached ADUs often uncover hidden issues in framing, utilities, drainage, or existing finishes. Many homeowners set aside roughly 10% to 20% of construction cost, with more for older homes or hillside sites.
